notes.front: What is Azure Cosmos DB?
notes.back: A fully managed NoSQL database service on Azure, offered as platform as a service.
notes.explanation: Microsoft runs the servers, patching, updates and backups, leaving you to write the application.
notes.example: Like renting a fully staffed archive for flexible records: you hand in and ask for files, and the staff handle the building.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, What is Azure Cosmos DB?
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a Cosmos DB container?
notes.back: The place in an Azure Cosmos DB database where data is stored, and the unit that scales.
notes.explanation: Data is stored on one or more partitions beneath it, which grow as throughput or storage increases.
notes.example: Like one filing cabinet in the archive: it holds the records and can be given more drawers as they grow.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Databases, containers, and items in Azure Cosmos DB”, Azure Cosmos DB containers
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Azure Cosmos DB, what is an item?
notes.back: An individual data entity stored inside a Cosmos DB container.
notes.explanation: Depending on the interface used, an item may be called a document, a row, a node or an edge.
notes.example: Like a single customer record: one JSON document with that customer’s name, email and address.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, How Azure Cosmos DB organizes data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Azure Cosmos DB, what is a logical partition?
notes.back: The set of items in a container that share the same partition key value.
notes.explanation: New logical partitions appear automatically as items with new key values are added.
notes.example: Like the drawer for surnames beginning “M” in a card index: every card with that initial goes in it.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Partitioning and horizontal scaling in Azure Cosmos DB”, Logical partitions
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does strong consistency guarantee in Azure Cosmos DB?
notes.back: Every read returns the most recent committed version of an item; no reader sees an uncommitted or partial write.
notes.explanation: This is the linearizability guarantee, the strictest of the five levels.
notes.example: Like a single shared whiteboard: whoever looks sees the last thing written, whichever door they came in by.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Strong consistency
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does bounded staleness guarantee in Azure Cosmos DB?
notes.back: Reads in any region lag writes by less than a set number of versions or a set time, whichever comes first.
notes.explanation: You choose the bound, so the maximum staleness is known in advance.
notes.example: Like a scoreboard promised never to be more than two goals or five minutes behind the match.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Bounded staleness consistency
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does session consistency guarantee in Azure Cosmos DB?
notes.back: Within one client session, reads honour read-your-writes and write-follows-reads.
notes.explanation: The client carries a session token after each write so later reads never see older data for that session.
notes.example: Like posting a comment and always seeing it yourself on refresh, even if a friend elsewhere sees it a moment later.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Session consistency
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does consistent prefix guarantee in Azure Cosmos DB?
notes.back: Writes made together in a transaction are always seen together and never out of order.
notes.explanation: The documentation adds that single-document writes under this level see eventual consistency.
notes.example: Like reading a serialised novel late: you may be chapters behind, but you never get chapter 9 before chapter 8 of the same instalment.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Consistent prefix consistency
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is eventual consistency in Azure Cosmos DB?
notes.back: The weakest level: a read may hit a lagging replica and return stale or no data.
notes.explanation: A client might even read values older than ones it read before.
notes.example: Like village gossip: everyone hears the news in the end, but not in the same order or at the same time.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Eventual consistency
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a Request Unit (RU) in Azure Cosmos DB?
notes.back: A performance currency that expresses the cost of any database operation as one normalised number.
notes.explanation: It abstracts the processing, input/output and memory an operation needs, whether a write, point read or query.
notes.example: Like a single pricing unit at a print shop, where colour, paper and binding all convert into “credits”.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Request Units in Azure Cosmos DB”, Overview
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is autoscale throughput in Azure Cosmos DB?
notes.back: An option where you set a maximum RU/s and the service adjusts capacity within that range to meet demand.
notes.explanation: Capacity follows actual use rather than staying at one fixed figure.
notes.example: Like a taxi firm that calls in drivers up to an agreed maximum as bookings rise.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, Throughput modes and pricing
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL?
notes.back: The native Cosmos DB interface: it stores data as JSON documents and is queried with a SQL-like syntax.
notes.explanation: Being native, it is the one the training recommends for new applications.
notes.example: Like writing `SELECT * FROM orders o WHERE o.status = "open"` against a store of JSON order documents.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for NoSQL
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB?
notes.back: A Cosmos DB interface compatible with MongoDB drivers and client libraries.
notes.explanation: Existing MongoDB applications can connect to it without significant code changes.
notes.example: Like a new hotel that accepts the key cards of your old one, so guests walk straight in.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for MongoDB
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Binary JSON (BSON)?
notes.back: A binary encoding of JSON, the format Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB stores data in.
notes.explanation: The data is still JSON-shaped; only the encoding on disk is binary.
notes.example: Like a zipped copy of a text file: same content, stored in a machine-friendly form.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for MongoDB
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the MongoDB Query Language (MQL)?
notes.back: The compact, object-oriented query syntax used with Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB, calling methods on collection objects.
notes.explanation: Instead of SQL statements, you call methods such as a find on a named collection.
notes.example: Like writing `db.books.find({author: "Austen"})` to fetch every Austen record.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for MongoDB
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Azure Cosmos DB for Table?
notes.back: A Cosmos DB interface that stores key-value data in tables, using the same programming model as Azure Table Storage.
notes.explanation: Applications already written for Table Storage can switch to it with minimal code changes.
notes.example: Like moving a card-index business into a bigger, faster building while keeping the same index cards.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for Table
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra?
notes.back: A Cosmos DB interface compatible with Apache Cassandra, an open-source column-family database.
notes.explanation: It suits teams moving an existing Cassandra workload to a fully managed cloud database.
notes.example: Like a phone company pointing its existing Cassandra app at a managed cloud database, so it no longer runs its own Cassandra servers.
introduces: Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra

notes.front: What is Cassandra Query Language (CQL)?
notes.back: The query language of Apache Cassandra, with a syntax similar to SQL.
notes.explanation: Someone who already writes SQL queries will find its statements familiar.
notes.example: Like writing `SELECT * FROM Readings WHERE SensorID = 7` against a Cassandra table.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra

notes.front: What is Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin?
notes.back: A Cosmos DB interface for graph data, queried with the Gremlin language.
notes.explanation: Graphs help when the connections between data matter as much as the data itself.
notes.example: Like a map of who follows whom on a social network, stored so you can walk from person to person.
introduces: Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin

notes.front: In a graph in Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin, what is a vertex?
notes.back: A node that represents an entity, such as an employee or a department.
notes.explanation: Vertices are the things; the lines between them are stored separately.
notes.example: Like a town on a road map.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin

notes.front: In a graph in Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin, what is an edge?
notes.back: A relationship between two vertices, such as “reports to”.
notes.explanation: Edges let a query travel from one entity to related ones.
notes.example: Like the road that joins two towns on a map.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which operational tasks does Microsoft handle for you in Azure Cosmos DB?
notes.back: Server provisioning, patching, updates and backups.
notes.explanation: As a PaaS offering, the underlying infrastructure is Microsoft’s job, not yours.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, What is Azure Cosmos DB?
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Must items in the same Cosmos DB container share one structure?
notes.back: No: Cosmos DB is schema-agnostic, so one item may have five properties and another fifteen different ones.
notes.explanation: That flexibility suits data whose shape changes over time or varies between records.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, What is Azure Cosmos DB?
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the Cosmos DB resource hierarchy, what is the account, and how many databases can it hold?
notes.back: The top-level Azure resource; it can hold unlimited databases.
notes.explanation: Everything else, from databases to items, sits beneath the account.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, How Azure Cosmos DB organizes data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Azure Cosmos DB, what is a database?
notes.back: A namespace that groups a set of Cosmos DB containers.
notes.explanation: It sits between the account and the containers, grouping related containers together.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Databases, containers, and items in Azure Cosmos DB”, Azure Cosmos DB databases
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: At which level of the Cosmos DB hierarchy do you set the partition key, throughput and indexing policy?
notes.back: The Cosmos DB container.
notes.explanation: The training calls the container the primary unit of storage and scaling.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, How Azure Cosmos DB organizes data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: From top to bottom, Azure Cosmos DB organises data as account, then database, then {{c1::container}}, then item.
notes.explanation: You create databases inside the account and containers inside the databases to store your data.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Databases, containers, and items in Azure Cosmos DB”, Elements in an Azure Cosmos DB account
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB, what is an item called?
notes.back: A document.
notes.explanation: The documentation maps the generic Cosmos DB item to each interface’s own word.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Databases, containers, and items in Azure Cosmos DB”, Azure Cosmos DB items
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does a Cosmos DB container scale, compared with most relational databases?
notes.back: It scales out across partitions, rather than up onto larger virtual machines.
notes.explanation: Partitions increase with throughput or grow as storage grows, giving unlimited throughput and storage for a container.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Databases, containers, and items in Azure Cosmos DB”, Azure Cosmos DB containers
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which item properties does Azure Cosmos DB index by default?
notes.back: All of them: indexes are created and maintained automatically.
notes.explanation: You need neither a schema up front nor manual index management, though a container’s indexing policy can be customised.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, How Azure Cosmos DB organizes data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What must you supply when you create a Cosmos DB container?
notes.back: A partition key: a property of the items used to spread data across partitions.
notes.explanation: Cosmos DB uses its value to route each write, update or delete to the right partition.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Databases, containers, and items in Azure Cosmos DB”, Azure Cosmos DB containers
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Each logical partition in Azure Cosmos DB can store up to {{c1::20 gigabytes}} of data.
notes.explanation: There is no limit on the number of logical partitions, only on the size of each one.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Partitioning and horizontal scaling in Azure Cosmos DB”, Logical partitions
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What uniquely identifies an item in a Cosmos DB container?
notes.back: Its partition key combined with its item ID, which is unique within the partition.
notes.explanation: The ID alone needs to be unique only inside its own logical partition.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Partitioning and horizontal scaling in Azure Cosmos DB”, Overview
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What range of values should a good Cosmos DB partition key have?
notes.back: A wide range: high cardinality, with many distinct values.
notes.explanation: A wide range of values is what lets the container keep scaling.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Partitioning and horizontal scaling in Azure Cosmos DB”, Choose a partition key
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides many values, how should a good partition key spread the workload?
notes.back: Evenly: RU consumption and data storage spread across all logical partitions.
notes.explanation: An even spread across logical partitions gives an even spread across the physical partitions beneath them.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Partitioning and horizontal scaling in Azure Cosmos DB”, Choose a partition key
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What happens when a partition key sends too many requests to a few partitions?
notes.back: Those partitions become “hot”, wasting provisioned throughput and possibly causing rate limiting and higher costs.
notes.explanation: Provisioned throughput is divided evenly among physical partitions, so uneven requests use it inefficiently.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Partitioning and horizontal scaling in Azure Cosmos DB”, Physical partitions
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Can you change a container’s partition key after you choose it?
notes.back: Not in place: you must move the data to a new container with the new key.
notes.explanation: The guidance also says the key should be a property whose value doesn’t change.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Partitioning and horizontal scaling in Azure Cosmos DB”, Choose a partition key
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When can you add Azure regions to a Cosmos DB account, and what happens to the data?
notes.back: At any time; the service automatically replicates the data to each new region.
notes.explanation: The documentation adds that the application needs no pause or redeployment to add or remove a region.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, Global distribution and performance
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a globally distributed Cosmos DB account, which replica do users read from and write to?
notes.back: The nearest regional replica.
notes.explanation: Serving each user from nearby keeps latency low wherever they are.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, Global distribution and performance
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What read and write availability does Azure Cosmos DB offer for multi-region databases?
notes.explanation: If one region is unavailable, the other regions handle application requests automatically.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Distribute data globally with Azure Cosmos DB”, Key benefits of global distribution
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which of the five Cosmos DB consistency levels is the strongest?
notes.back: Strong consistency.
notes.explanation: The levels run from strong, through bounded staleness, session and consistent prefix, to eventual.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Overview
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Cosmos DB consistency level is the weakest?
notes.back: Eventual consistency.
notes.explanation: The training adds that it gives the highest availability of the five.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Eventual consistency
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: From strongest to weakest, the Cosmos DB levels are strong, {{c1::bounded staleness}}, session, consistent prefix and eventual.
notes.explanation: It is the one level that lets you set how far behind reads may fall.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Overview
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: From strongest to weakest, the Cosmos DB levels are strong, bounded staleness, session, {{c1::consistent prefix}} and eventual.
notes.explanation: It sits just above eventual, adding an ordering guarantee for transactional writes.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Overview
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the Cosmos DB order of consistency levels, {{c1::session}} consistency sits in the middle, between bounded staleness and consistent prefix.
notes.explanation: It is also the most widely used of the five.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Overview
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which consistency level is the most widely used for single-region and globally distributed applications?
notes.back: Session consistency.
notes.explanation: It gives write latency, availability and read throughput comparable to eventual consistency, with guarantees suited to user-centred apps.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Session consistency
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: For most transactional applications, which consistency level does the training recommend starting with?
notes.back: Session consistency.
notes.explanation: It is the recommended starting point, which you can then tighten or relax.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, Global distribution and performance
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In bounded staleness, what two ways can you set the maximum staleness?
notes.back: By a number of versions of an item, or by a time interval.
notes.explanation: Whichever limit is reached first applies.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Bounded staleness consistency
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When is eventual consistency the ideal choice?
notes.back: When the application needs no ordering guarantees, such as counts of likes.
notes.explanation: Where order doesn’t matter, the weakest guarantee is enough.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Eventual consistency
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Where is a Cosmos DB default consistency level set, and what does it apply to?
notes.back: On the account, at any time; it applies to all databases and containers in that account.
notes.explanation: Reads and queries use it unless a client overrides it.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Configure the default consistency level
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How many Request Units does reading a single item of about 1 kilobyte by its ID and partition key use?
notes.back: One.
notes.explanation: Writes and queries are measured in the same unit, whatever the interface.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Request Units in Azure Cosmos DB”, Overview
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does item size affect the RUs used to read or write an item?
notes.back: Larger items consume more RUs.
notes.explanation: Size is one of several factors, along with indexing and property count.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Request Units in Azure Cosmos DB”, Request Unit considerations
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Cosmos DB operations consume Request Units?
notes.back: Every operation: reads, writes, queries and deletes.
notes.explanation: One metric therefore covers both performance and cost.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, Throughput modes and pricing
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In which Cosmos DB throughput mode is throughput reserved exclusively for a single container?
notes.back: Dedicated throughput.
notes.explanation: The documentation adds that the container receives that throughput all the time, backed by service-level agreements.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, Throughput modes and pricing
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In which Cosmos DB throughput mode is throughput provisioned at the database level and shared by its containers?
notes.back: Shared throughput.
notes.explanation: No container has a guaranteed share, so a busy container can affect the others.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, Throughput modes and pricing
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In which Cosmos DB throughput mode do you provision nothing up front and pay per request?
notes.back: Serverless.
notes.explanation: You are billed for the RUs your operations consume and for the storage your data uses.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, Throughput modes and pricing
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A shared-throughput Cosmos DB database is limited to {{c1::25}} containers.
notes.explanation: Containers beyond that must have their own dedicated throughput.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Introduction to provisioned throughput in Azure Cosmos DB”, Set throughput on a database
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How many Azure regions can a serverless Cosmos DB account run in?
notes.back: Only one; regions can’t be added after the account is created.
notes.explanation: Global distribution across regions therefore needs a provisioned throughput account.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Azure Cosmos DB serverless account type”, Use serverless resources
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which traffic pattern best fits the Cosmos DB serverless option?
notes.back: Intermittent, unpredictable traffic with long idle times.
notes.explanation: Provisioning capacity for such traffic isn’t needed and might cost too much.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Azure Cosmos DB serverless account type”, Use cases
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does Azure Cosmos DB offer Internet of Things and telemetry systems?
notes.back: Fast ingestion of high-frequency device data, available for near-real-time processing.
notes.explanation: Device data arrives in bursts from sensors in many places.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, When to use Cosmos DB
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Cosmos DB use case covers player profiles, leaderboards and in-game stats?
notes.back: Gaming.
notes.explanation: These need single-digit millisecond response times.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, When to use Cosmos DB
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Cosmos DB use case covers product catalogues, shopping carts and order pipelines?
notes.back: Retail and e-commerce.
notes.explanation: The use-cases page notes that catalogue attributes can vary and change over time.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, When to use Cosmos DB
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Cosmos DB use case covers personalised user experiences, social features and third-party integrations?
notes.back: Web and mobile apps.
notes.explanation: The documentation adds that it is well suited to modelling social interactions.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, When to use Cosmos DB
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: If an application depends on complex multi-table joins, which service does the training suggest instead of Cosmos DB?
notes.back: Azure SQL Database.
notes.explanation: Cosmos DB is a strong fit for flexible schemas and global reach, not for heavy relational joins.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, When to use Cosmos DB
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: For large-scale historical analytics, what does the training suggest instead of Cosmos DB?
notes.back: Microsoft Fabric, or Azure Synapse Analytics.
notes.explanation: The current exam outline names Fabric; Synapse appears in older material and is covered in the next topic.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, When to use Cosmos DB
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which data interfaces (APIs) does Azure Cosmos DB support? Name two.
notes.back: Any two of: NoSQL, MongoDB, Table, Apache Cassandra, Apache Gremlin.
notes.explanation: Each is designed for a different type of data or use case.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Why Cosmos DB supports multiple APIs
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra
Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin

notes.front: When do you choose which interface a Cosmos DB account uses?
notes.back: When you create the account.
notes.explanation: The choice fixes the data format, query language and client libraries the application works with.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Why Cosmos DB supports multiple APIs
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the training name as the main benefit of Cosmos DB’s multiple interfaces?
notes.back: Portability: existing MongoDB or Cassandra applications can move with minimal code changes.
notes.explanation: Moving also brings global distribution and managed throughput.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Why Cosmos DB supports multiple APIs
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What was Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL called before 2023?
notes.back: The `SQL API`.
notes.explanation: Older material that uses the old name means the same service.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for NoSQL
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Cosmos DB interface does the training recommend for new applications?
notes.back: Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL.
notes.explanation: It is the native interface, storing JSON documents.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for NoSQL
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Cosmos DB interface supports mirroring operational data into Microsoft Fabric without a pipeline?
notes.back: Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL.
notes.explanation: Analytics can then run on live data without affecting the transactional workload.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for NoSQL
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB, what format is data stored in and which language queries it?
notes.back: Binary JSON (BSON), queried with the MongoDB Query Language (MQL).
notes.explanation: The training calls this interface a natural choice for teams with MongoDB expertise.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for MongoDB
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does Azure Cosmos DB for Table add over Azure Table Storage? Name two.
notes.back: Any two of: greater scalability, global distribution, automatic secondary indexes, instant autoscale.
notes.explanation: The data model stays the same key-value tables, so the gains come without rewriting the app.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for Table
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Is Azure Table Storage still supported, and which service is recommended for new key-value workloads at scale?
notes.back: Yes, it is still supported; Azure Cosmos DB for Table is recommended for new workloads.
notes.explanation: The Azure Storage documentation likewise says Table Storage is now part of Azure Cosmos DB.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for Table
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Azure Cosmos DB for Table, what identifies each entity (row)?
notes.back: A unique combination of partition key and row key.
notes.explanation: It is the same keying scheme as Azure Table Storage.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “What is Azure Cosmos DB for Table?”, Overview
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the column-family tables used by Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra, must every row have the same columns?
notes.back: No; rows don’t have to contain the same columns.
notes.explanation: That is unlike a relational table, where the schema is fixed for all rows.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra

notes.front: Which kinds of application does the training give for graph data in Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin? Name two.
notes.back: Any two of: social networks, recommendation engines, fraud detection, organisational hierarchies.
notes.explanation: In each, the connections between data are as important as the data itself.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin

notes.front: A start-up is building a brand-new app on Cosmos DB, storing JSON orders and querying them with SQL-like statements. Which interface should it choose?
notes.choices:
A) Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
B) Azure Cosmos DB for Table
C) Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra
D) Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin
notes.back: A: Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL.
notes.explanation: It is the native interface, stores JSON documents with SQL-like queries, and is recommended for new applications.
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because Table stores key-value pairs. C is wrong because Cassandra suits migrating Cassandra workloads. D is wrong because Gremlin is for graphs.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for NoSQL
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin

notes.front: A team runs an app built on MongoDB drivers and wants a managed cloud database with as few code changes as possible. Which interface fits?
notes.choices:
A) Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin
B) Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
C) Azure Cosmos DB for Table
D) Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB
notes.back: D: Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB.
notes.explanation: It is compatible with MongoDB drivers and client libraries, so existing apps connect without significant changes.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because Gremlin is for graph data. B is wrong because the app would have to be rewritten for the native interface. C is wrong because Table expects the Table Storage model.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for MongoDB
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin

notes.front: An app on Azure Table Storage now needs global distribution and automatic secondary indexes, with minimal code change. Where should it move?
notes.choices:
A) Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra
B) Azure Cosmos DB for Table
C) Azure SQL Database
D) Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB
notes.back: B: Azure Cosmos DB for Table.
notes.explanation: It uses the same programming model as Table Storage and adds global distribution and automatic secondary indexes.
notes.choicesExplained: A and D are wrong because they need Cassandra or MongoDB clients. C is wrong because it is relational and would need a redesign.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for Table

notes.front: A telecoms firm runs an Apache Cassandra cluster with CQL queries and wants to stop managing servers. Which interface should it pick?
notes.choices:
A) Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
B) Azure Cosmos DB for Table
C) Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin
D) Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra
notes.back: D: Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra.
notes.explanation: It is compatible with Apache Cassandra and suits teams migrating a Cassandra workload to a fully managed database.
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are wrong because neither speaks CQL. C is wrong because Gremlin is for graph traversal.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra

notes.front: A bank wants to trace chains of transfers between accounts to spot fraud rings, following links several steps deep. Which interface fits?
notes.choices:
A) Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin
B) Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB
C) Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
D) Azure Cosmos DB for Table
notes.back: A: Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin.
notes.explanation: Graph data with vertices and edges suits cases like fraud detection, where the connections matter as much as the data.
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong because document stores aren’t built for traversing relationships. D is wrong because key-value tables don’t model links.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin

notes.front: A team created a Cosmos DB account for NoSQL, then decides it must use its existing MongoDB drivers. What should it do?
notes.choices:
A) Change the account’s interface setting
B) Change the consistency level
C) Create a new account for MongoDB and move the data
D) Add a region
notes.back: C: create a new account for MongoDB and move the data.
notes.explanation: The interface is chosen when the account is created, and that choice fixes the drivers and query language it works with.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because the interface is set at creation. B and D are wrong because consistency and regions don’t change the interface.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Why Cosmos DB supports multiple APIs
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A 2021 tutorial tells you to create a Cosmos DB account using the `SQL API`. Which interface do you pick today?
notes.choices:
A) Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
B) Azure SQL Database
C) Azure Cosmos DB for Table
D) Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra
notes.back: A: Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL.
notes.explanation: The old name was changed to NoSQL in 2023, and it is the same service.
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because it is a separate relational service. C and D are wrong because they are different interfaces with their own data models.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for NoSQL

notes.front: A video site shows a like counter that may lag a little and needs no ordering. It wants the highest availability. Which consistency level fits?
notes.choices:
A) Bounded staleness
B) Strong
C) Eventual
D) Session
notes.back: C: eventual consistency.
notes.explanation: Eventual consistency is ideal where no ordering guarantees are needed, such as counts of likes.
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are wrong because they give freshness guarantees the like counter doesn’t need. D is wrong because no per-user session guarantee is needed.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Eventual consistency
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a social app, users must always see their own new posts after refreshing, but it is fine if friends see them a moment later. Which level is enough?
notes.choices:
A) Strong
B) Consistent prefix
C) Eventual
D) Session
notes.back: D: session consistency.
notes.explanation: Session consistency guarantees read-your-writes within a client session, with throughput close to eventual.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because every reader needn’t see the latest write. B and C are wrong because neither guarantees users see their own writes.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Session consistency
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A ticketing system must never sell a seat twice: every read, from any region, must show the latest committed booking. Which level is required?
notes.choices:
A) Consistent prefix
B) Strong
C) Eventual
D) Session
notes.back: B: strong consistency.
notes.explanation: Only strong consistency guarantees every read returns the most recent committed version.
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wrong because readers may see stale data. D is wrong because it only guarantees a client’s own writes.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Strong consistency
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A stock dashboard read in three regions may be slightly behind, but never by more than five seconds. Which level lets you set that limit?
notes.choices:
A) Session
B) Bounded staleness
C) Eventual
D) Consistent prefix
notes.back: B: bounded staleness.
notes.explanation: Bounded staleness caps how far reads lag, by versions or by time.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because it guarantees only a client’s own session. C and D are wrong because they set no maximum lag.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Bounded staleness consistency
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An app writes an order and its payment in one transaction. Readers may see slightly old data, but must never see the payment without its order. Which is the weakest level that guarantees this?
notes.choices:
A) Eventual
B) Consistent prefix
C) Strong
D) Session
notes.back: B: consistent prefix.
notes.explanation: Writes in one transaction are always visible together, never out of order, under consistent prefix.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because it gives no ordering guarantee. D and C are stronger than needed; the question asks for the weakest.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Consistent prefix consistency
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A developer is trying Cosmos DB for a hobby app used a few times a day, in one region, and wants no charge for idle capacity. Which mode fits?
notes.choices:
A) Dedicated throughput
B) Serverless
C) Shared throughput
D) Autoscale throughput
notes.back: B: serverless.
notes.explanation: Serverless suits getting started and intermittent traffic, billing only for RUs consumed and storage.
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wrong because provisioned throughput is billed whether used or not. D is wrong because autoscale still provisions a range of capacity.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Azure Cosmos DB serverless account type”, Use cases
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A retailer with a serverless Cosmos DB account now needs replicas in Europe and Asia. What must it do?
notes.choices:
A) Use a provisioned throughput account
B) Switch the consistency level to strong
C) Add the regions to the serverless account
D) Raise the RU/s limit
notes.back: A: use a provisioned throughput account.
notes.explanation: A serverless account runs in one region only, and regions can’t be added after creation.
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because consistency doesn’t create replicas. C is wrong because serverless accounts can’t add regions. D is wrong because serverless has no RU/s setting.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Azure Cosmos DB serverless account type”, Use serverless resources
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A SaaS vendor gives each of 12 small customers its own container and wants them to share one pool of throughput to save money. Which mode fits?
notes.choices:
A) Dedicated throughput on each container
B) Shared throughput at the database level
C) Serverless in six regions
D) Strong consistency
notes.back: B: shared throughput at the database level.
notes.explanation: Sharing a database’s throughput across containers suits multitenant apps with one container per tenant, up to 25 containers.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because dedicated throughput is reserved and billed per container. C is wrong because serverless runs in one region. D is wrong because consistency is not a throughput mode.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Introduction to provisioned throughput in Azure Cosmos DB”, Set throughput on a database
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A container holds millions of shopping-basket items for users worldwide. Which partition key follows the guidance best?
notes.choices:
A) User ID
B) Order status
C) Country
D) Currency
notes.back: A: user ID.
notes.explanation: A user ID has many distinct values that spread storage and requests evenly across logical partitions.
notes.choicesExplained: C, B and D are wrong because each has few distinct values, the low-cardinality pattern that creates hot partitions and can push a partition towards the 20-gigabyte limit.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Partitioning and horizontal scaling in Azure Cosmos DB”, Choose a partition key
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A container uses “storeId” as its partition key, and its items carry 300 distinct store IDs. How many logical partitions does it have?
notes.choices:
A) 1
B) 25
C) It depends on the RU/s
D) 300
notes.explanation: Each distinct partition key value forms one logical partition.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because items with different values don’t share a partition. B confuses this with the shared-throughput container limit. C is wrong because logical partitions follow key values, not throughput.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Partitioning and horizontal scaling in Azure Cosmos DB”, Overview
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A payroll system relies on complex queries joining employees, grades, tax bands and pensions across many tables. Which service suits it best?
notes.choices:
A) Azure SQL Database
B) Azure Cosmos DB for Table
C) Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin
D) Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL
notes.back: A: Azure SQL Database.
notes.explanation: The training names complex multi-table joins as a poor fit for Cosmos DB and points to Azure SQL Database.
notes.choicesExplained: D, B and C are wrong because each is a Cosmos DB interface, and Cosmos DB isn’t suited to heavy multi-table joins.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, When to use Cosmos DB
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A mobile game needs a global leaderboard answering in a few milliseconds for players on every continent. Is Cosmos DB a good fit?
notes.choices:
A) Yes: gaming with low latency and global reach is a named use case
B) No: it only runs in one region
C) No: it can’t store changing records
D) Only if the data is stored in the archive tier
notes.back: A: yes; gaming is a named use case.
notes.explanation: The training lists leaderboards needing single-digit millisecond responses, and Cosmos DB replicates to any region.
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because only serverless accounts are single-region. C is wrong because it is schema-agnostic. D is wrong because access tiers belong to Blob Storage.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, When to use Cosmos DB
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A product catalogue has books with ISBNs and shirts with sizes and colours, all in one container. How does Cosmos DB treat the differing fields?
notes.choices:
A) It accepts them: containers are schema-agnostic
B) It rejects items that don’t match the first item
C) It needs one container per shape
D) It stores extra fields as NULL columns
notes.back: A: it accepts them; containers are schema-agnostic.
notes.explanation: Items in the same container needn’t share a structure, which suits records that vary.
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong because no shared schema is enforced. D is wrong because there are no fixed columns to fill.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, What is Azure Cosmos DB?
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A developer asks which indexes to create before querying a new Cosmos DB container by any property. What is the answer?
notes.choices:
A) None: every property is indexed automatically by default
B) Only the partition key is ever indexed
C) One per property, created by hand
D) Indexes need a relational schema first
notes.back: A: none; every property is indexed automatically.
notes.explanation: Cosmos DB creates and maintains indexes on all item properties by default.
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because all properties are indexed. C is wrong because manual index management isn’t needed. D is wrong because no schema is needed.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, How Azure Cosmos DB organizes data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A two-person team wants a NoSQL database but has no one to provision servers, apply patches or run backups. Why does Azure Cosmos DB suit them?
notes.choices:
A) They must install it on their own virtual machines
B) It needs a dedicated database administrator
C) It only runs on premises
D) Microsoft handles that infrastructure work as part of the service
notes.back: D: Microsoft handles that infrastructure work.
notes.explanation: As a fully managed PaaS service, Cosmos DB leaves provisioning, patching, updates and backups to Microsoft.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because there are no virtual machines to manage. B is wrong because the operational overhead is handled for you. C is wrong because it is an Azure cloud service.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, What is Azure Cosmos DB?
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A designer wants one group of items to have its own partition key, throughput and indexing policy. Which Cosmos DB resource should she create?
notes.choices:
A) A new account
B) A new logical partition
C) A new item
D) A new Cosmos DB container
notes.back: D: a new Cosmos DB container.
notes.explanation: Partition key, throughput and indexing policy are all configured at the container level, the unit of storage and scaling.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because an account sits above these settings. B is wrong because logical partitions form automatically from key values. C is wrong because an item is a single entity.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Describe Azure Cosmos DB”, How Azure Cosmos DB organizes data
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An online shop with a provisioned Cosmos DB account in one region gains many customers in Australia. What is the simplest way to cut their latency?
notes.choices:
A) Export the data nightly to a second account
B) Rebuild the app on Azure Table Storage
C) Switch to serverless
D) Add an Australian region to the account
notes.back: D: add an Australian region to the account.
notes.explanation: Regions can be added at any time without redeploying, and data replicates to them so users read from nearby.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because replication is built in. B is wrong because it adds work without reducing distance. C is wrong because serverless is single-region.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Distribute data globally with Azure Cosmos DB”, Overview
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Two point reads use the same ID and partition key lookup; one item is 1 kilobyte, the other 50 kilobytes. Which costs more RUs?
notes.choices:
A) Neither: reads are free
B) The 1-kilobyte read
C) Both cost 1 RU
D) The 50-kilobyte read
notes.back: D: the 50-kilobyte read.
notes.explanation: As item size increases, the RUs consumed to read it increase too.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because every operation uses RUs. B is wrong because the smaller item costs less. C is wrong because 1 RU is the figure for about 1 kilobyte.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Request Units in Azure Cosmos DB”, Request Unit considerations
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Strong versus eventual consistency: what does a read return under each?
notes.back: Strong: always the latest committed write. Eventual: possibly stale or no data from a lagging replica.
notes.explanation: They are the two ends of the five-level scale.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Overview
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Session consistency versus consistent prefix: whose view does each protect?
notes.back: Session: one client sees its own writes. Consistent prefix: every reader sees transactional writes in order.
notes.explanation: One is a per-client guarantee; the other is about order for all readers.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB”, Overview
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Dedicated versus shared throughput: who gets the RU/s?
notes.back: Dedicated: one container, guaranteed. Shared: up to 25 containers in a database, with no guaranteed share each.
notes.explanation: Dedicated protects a busy container; shared saves money across many small ones.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Introduction to provisioned throughput in Azure Cosmos DB”, Overview
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Serverless versus provisioned throughput in Cosmos DB: how are you billed, and can you go multi-region?
notes.back: Serverless: per RU consumed, one region only. Provisioned: per RU/s reserved, and regions can be added.
notes.explanation: Serverless costs are less predictable because they follow the number of requests.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Azure Cosmos DB serverless account type”, Overview
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Logical versus physical partition in Cosmos DB: what is each?
notes.back: Logical: items sharing a partition key value. Physical: an internal unit, managed by Cosmos DB, holding one or more logical partitions.
notes.explanation: You design logical partitions through your key choice; physical ones are the service’s concern.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Partitioning and horizontal scaling in Azure Cosmos DB”, Physical partitions
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Azure Cosmos DB for Table versus Azure Table Storage: what stays the same, and what changes?
notes.back: Same: key-value tables and programming model. Changes: Cosmos DB adds scale, global distribution, secondary indexes and instant autoscale.
notes.explanation: This is why existing Table Storage apps can move with minimal code changes.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn training, “Identify Azure Cosmos DB APIs”, Cosmos DB for Table
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
